entry: Genus of about 35 species of mostly deciduous trees and shrubs in the birch family, Betulaceae. The genus *Alnus* is found throughout the north temperate zone, with a few species reaching [[Central America]] and the northern and southern [[Andes]]. Alders bear male and female catkins on the same plant. Unlike [[Birch|birches]], their female catkins are woody and open to release seeds, much like conifer cones. The largest species, red alder (*A. rubra*) of the west coast of North America and black alder (*A. glutinosa*) of Europe, reach over 30 m (100 ft). Alders form root nodules with the nitrogen-fixing bacterium *Frankia alni*, which absorbs nitrogen from the air and makes it available to the tree, receiving sugars from [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] in return. Red alder stands supply between 130 and 320 kilograms per hectare (120 and 290 pounds per acre) of [[Nitrogen|nitrogen]] to the soil each year.

Two German multinational family-owned discount supermarket chains. Founded by brothers Karl and Theo Albrecht in 1946, when they took over their mother's store in Essen. The business was split in 1960 into Aldi Nord, based in Essen and initially operating in northern [[West Germany]], and Aldi Süd, based in Mülheim. The two groups divided global markets between them, except in the United States, where Aldi Süd operates under the Aldi name and Aldi Nord owns Trader Joe's. Together they operate over 13,600 stores in 18 countries.

English writer and philosopher. Huxley wrote nearly 50 books, including novels, essays, poetry and travel writing. He is known for the dystopian novel *Brave New World* (1932), which depicts a society kept stable through genetic manipulation and conditioning, and for *Island* (1962), his final novel, which presents a [[Utopia|utopia]]. A pacifist, he wrote on [[Mysticism|mysticism]] in *The Perennial Philosophy* (1945), and *The Doors of Perception* (1954) described his experience with [[Mescaline|mescaline]]. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature nine times. He lived in [[Los Angeles]] from 1937 until his death.

American actor and film producer. Baldwin played Jack Ryan in *The Hunt for Red October* (1990) and earned an Academy Award nomination for *The Cooler* (2003). From 2006 to 2013 he starred as Jack Donaghy on the [[NBC]] sitcom *30 Rock*, which earned him two Primetime Emmy Awards. He hosted *Saturday Night Live* a record 17 times, and his portrayal of [[Donald Trump]] won him a third Primetime Emmy in 2017. In 2021 Baldwin accidentally discharged a live round from a prop revolver on the set of the Western *Rust*, killing cinematographer Halyna Hutchins. The involuntary manslaughter charge against him was dismissed in July 2024.

English actor. Guinness began acting on stage in 1934 and joined the Old Vic in 1936. He became a star of postwar British film through six Ealing comedies, including *Kind Hearts and Coronets* (1949), in which he played eight characters. He won the Academy Award and BAFTA Award for Best Actor for Colonel Nicholson in *The Bridge on the River Kwai* (1957), and he collaborated six times with director [[David Lean]]. He played Obi-Wan Kenobi in the original *Star Wars* trilogy and George Smiley in the [[BBC]] series *Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy*. He was knighted by [[Elizabeth II]] in 1959.

English occultist, ceremonial magician and founder of the religion of Thelema. Crowley was also a poet, novelist, mountaineer and painter. Born into a wealthy family in Royal Leamington Spa, he rejected his parents' Plymouth Brethren faith and studied at Trinity College at the [[University of Cambridge]]. In 1904, in [[Cairo]], he wrote *The Book of the Law*, which he said had been dictated to him by an entity named Aiwass. The book announced the Æon of [[Horus]] and the principle "Do what thou wilt." In 1912 he joined the German-based Ordo Templi Orientis and became leader of its British branch. He founded the Abbey of Thelema, a religious commune in Cefalù, Sicily, in 1920, and the Italian government evicted him in 1923. During the [[World War I|First World War]] he lived in the United States. He is regarded as an influence on [[Western esotericism]] and the counterculture of the 1960s.

Mexican filmmaker of psychological dramas about the human condition. His films include *Amores perros* (2000), *Babel* (2006) and *Birdman* (2014). He won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Director for *Birdman* and for *The Revenant* (2015), becoming the third director to win the award back-to-back, after [[John Ford]] and Joseph L. Mankiewicz. He won the Best Director Award at the [[Cannes Film Festival]] in 2006. He also received a Special Achievement Academy Award for the virtual reality installation *Carne y Arena* (2017).

Cuban novelist, essayist and musicologist. Born in Lausanne, Switzerland, to French and Russian parents, Carpentier grew up in [[Havana]] and identified strongly as Cuban. He wrote journalism, radio drama, opera libretti and academic essays, but is best known for novels that helped shape the Latin American literary boom. He was among the first writers to use magical realism, which he called *lo real maravilloso* (the marvelous real). His novel *El reino de este mundo* (1949), about the [[Haitian Revolution]], is the most famous example. His style drew on the [[Baroque]] tradition and on Afro-Cuban music, and he adapted the theories of [[Surrealism]] to Latin American writing. Carpentier was jailed and exiled for his leftist politics and often aligned himself with revolutionary movements, including [[Fidel Castro]]'s revolution in Cuba.

Russian Greco-Roman wrestler and politician. Competing for the [[Soviet Union]] and later Russia, Karelin won Olympic gold medals in 1988, 1992 and 1996 and a silver in 2000. He had 887 wins and two losses in senior competition, both by a single point and both considered controversial. He won nine World Championship gold medals without losing a match, and FILA named him the greatest Greco-Roman wrestler of the 20th century. He was named a Hero of the Russian Federation in 1996. Karelin was elected to the State Duma in 1999 and served until 2020, when he entered the Federation Council as a senator.

Soviet-Russian author and dissident. Solzhenitsyn exposed political repression in the Soviet Union, especially the [[Gulag]] prison system. Serving as a captain in the Red Army during [[World War II]], he was arrested for criticizing [[Joseph Stalin]] in private correspondence and sentenced to eight years in the Gulag, followed by internal exile. His novel *One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich* (1962) was published with the approval of [[Nikita Khrushchev]]. His three-volume nonfiction work *The Gulag Archipelago* (1973) sold tens of millions of copies. He received the 1970 [[Nobel Prize]] in Literature. In 1974 he was stripped of Soviet citizenship and flown to West Germany, and in 1976 he settled in [[Vermont]]. His citizenship was restored in 1990, and he returned to Russia in 1994.

Infinite cardinal number used to measure the size of infinite sets, introduced by [[Georg Cantor]]. The smallest is ℵ₀ (aleph-null), the [[Cardinality|cardinality]] of the [[Natural number|natural numbers]] and of any countably infinite set. The next is ℵ₁, the smallest cardinality greater than ℵ₀. Unlike [[Infinity|infinity]] in calculus, which describes unbounded growth, the alephs measure the sizes of sets.

City in northern Syria, capital of Aleppo Governorate (pop., 2021: 2,098,000). It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, possibly occupied since the sixth millennium BC. It is first mentioned in cuneiform tablets from the late third millennium BC, when it was part of the [[Amorites|Amorite]] state of Yamhad. Its location at one end of the [[Silk Road]] made it a trading center between the Mediterranean and Mesopotamia. For centuries it was the third-largest city of the [[Ottoman Empire]], after [[Constantinople]] and [[Cairo]]. The opening of the [[Suez Canal]] in 1869 diverted much trade to sea, starting a slow decline. After World War I, Aleppo lost its northern hinterland to Turkey. In the [[Syrian civil war]], many parts of the city suffered massive destruction, and an estimated 31,000 people were killed in Aleppo during the conflict.

Italian chemist and physicist, pioneer of electricity. Volta is credited with inventing the [[Electric battery|electric battery]] in the form of the voltaic pile, which he reported in a two-part letter to the president of the Royal Society in London, published in 1800. The device showed that electricity could be generated chemically, disproving the view that it came only from living beings, and it helped found [[Electrochemistry|electrochemistry]]. He also discovered [[Methane|methane]]. [[Napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte]] admired his invention and honored him. Volta taught experimental physics at the University of Pavia for nearly 40 years. The SI unit of electric potential, the [[Volt|volt]], is named after him.

Chain of 14 main volcanic islands and 55 smaller ones, mostly part of the U.S. state of [[Alaska]]. The archipelago extends roughly 1,200 mi (1,900 km) west from the Alaska Peninsula, separating the [[Bering Sea]] from the [[Pacific Ocean]]. Its 57 [[Volcano|volcanoes]] form the northernmost part of the Pacific [[Ring of Fire]]. The islands were known as the Catherine Archipelago before 1867. The Commander Islands, farther west, belong to Russia. In June 1942 Japanese forces occupied Kiska and Attu, the only invasion of U.S. territory in North America during [[World War II]].

Scottish football manager and former player. Ferguson managed Manchester United from 1986 to 2013 and won 38 trophies with the club, including 13 [[Premier League]] titles, five FA Cups and two [[UEFA Champions League]] titles, in 1999 and 2008. The 1999 win completed the first continental treble by an English club. He had earlier led Aberdeen to three Scottish league championships. He was knighted in 1999 for services to football.

American rock climber known for free solo ascents, which are climbs made without ropes or protective gear. In June 2017 he became the first person to free solo the 880-meter (2,900 ft) Freerider route on El Capitan in [[Yosemite National Park]], graded 5.13a. In 2015 he and Tommy Caldwell won a *Piolet d'Or* for the Fitz Traverse of the Cerro Chaltén (Fitzroy) Group in [[Patagonia]]. In January 2026 he free soloed the Taipei 101 tower in [[Taipei]], Taiwan. Honnold is the subject of the 2018 documentary *Free Solo*, which won an Academy Award.

American political commentator and conspiracy theorist. Jones hosts *The Alex Jones Show* from [[Austin, Texas]] and founded the websites Infowars and Banned.Video, which promote conspiracy theories. He has alleged that the U.S. government concealed or falsified the [[Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting]] and the [[September 11 attacks]]. In October 2022, juries in Connecticut and Texas awarded a total of $1.487 billion in damages to a first responder and families of Sandy Hook victims over his falsehoods, and in December 2022 Jones filed for personal bankruptcy.

American former baseball shortstop and third baseman. Rodriguez played 22 seasons in [[Major League Baseball]], mainly for the Seattle Mariners, Texas Rangers and New York Yankees. He hit 696 home runs and won three American League Most Valuable Player Awards. In 2009 he admitted to using [[Steroid|steroids]] from 2001 to 2003, while with the Rangers. In 2013 he was suspended for 211 games over the Biogenesis scandal, and arbitration reduced the suspension to 162 games. He later worked as a broadcaster and as chief executive of A-Rod Corp.

Canadian-American [[Game show|game show]] host. Trebek hosted the quiz show *Jeopardy!* for 37 seasons, from its 1984 revival until his death, and was regarded as a pop culture icon. He began his career at the [[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]] in 1961. He became a naturalized American citizen in 1998 and received the Daytime Emmy Award for Outstanding Game Show Host eight times. In 2019 he disclosed that he had stage IV [[Pancreatic cancer|pancreatic cancer]], and he continued hosting while in treatment.

Slovak communist statesman, de facto leader of Czechoslovakia (1968–69). As First Secretary of the Communist Party from January 1968, Dubček led the [[Prague Spring]] reforms, a program of cultural and economic liberalization known by the slogan "socialism with a human face." In August 1968 half a million Soviet-led [[Warsaw Pact]] troops invaded Czechoslovakia, reversing the reforms. Dubček was forced to resign in April 1969 and was expelled from the Communist Party in 1970. During the 1989 Velvet Revolution he served as chairman of the federal assembly and contended for the presidency with [[Václav Havel]]. The [[European Parliament]] awarded him the Sakharov Prize that year.

Scottish physician and microbiologist. In 1928 Fleming noticed that a mold of the genus *Penicillium* on a culture plate had produced a substance that inhibited bacteria. The substance, later named benzylpenicillin, was the first [[Antibiotic|antibiotic]] discovered, and its discovery has been described as the "single greatest victory ever achieved over disease." Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain for the discovery of [[Penicillin|penicillin]]. He also discovered the [[Enzyme|enzyme]] lysozyme. During [[World War I]] he worked in battlefield hospitals and observed that antiseptics often worsened deep wounds. He was knighted in 1944.

Scottish-born Canadian-American inventor and engineer, credited with the first practical [[Telephone|telephone]]. Bell received the first U.S. patent for the telephone on March 7, 1876. His mother and wife were both deaf, and his research on hearing and speech led him to experiment with hearing devices. His other work included optical telecommunications, hydrofoils and aeronautics. He co-founded the American Telephone and Telegraph Company in 1885 and was the second president of the [[National Geographic|National Geographic Society]] from 1898 to 1903. He also studied [[Heredity|heredity]], which he considered his most notable contribution to basic science.

German-born French mathematician. Grothendieck was the leading figure in the creation of modern [[Algebraic geometry|algebraic geometry]], adding [[Commutative algebra|commutative algebra]], [[Homological algebra|homological algebra]], [[Sheaf (mathematics)|sheaf theory]] and [[Category theory|category theory]] to its foundations. He was awarded the [[Fields Medal]] in 1966. He worked at the Institut des hautes études scientifiques from 1958 until 1970, when he left over a dispute about military funding. He later taught at the University of Montpellier, withdrew from the mathematical community to pursue political and religious interests, and from 1991 lived in seclusion in the [[Pyrenees]]. Many consider him the greatest mathematician of the 20th century.

American Founding Father and first U.S. secretary of the treasury (1789–95). Hamilton served as aide-de-camp to [[George Washington]] during the [[American Revolutionary War|Revolutionary War]] and fought at the [[Siege of Yorktown]]. He wrote 51 of the 85 *Federalist Papers* in support of ratifying the Constitution. As treasury secretary he established the First Bank of the United States. He was a founder of the [[Federalist Party]], and in 1804 he died after being mortally wounded in a duel with [[Aaron Burr]].

Emperor of Russia, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Finland (r. 1881–94). Alexander pursued highly reactionary domestic policies, known as the counter-reforms, which reversed some of the liberal reforms of his father, Alexander II. Russia fought no major wars during his reign, and he became known as "The Peacemaker." His major foreign policy achievement was the Franco-Russian Alliance, which later drew Russia into [[World War I]]. His political legacy posed a direct challenge to the European order set forth by [[Otto von Bismarck]].
